title: Reformation Day (31 October)
hookLine: Lutherans and others remember 1517, now often with Catholic neighbors

cards: What does it take for a church to say, out loud, we need fixing? On the last day of October, while some streets fill with costumes and pumpkins, Lutheran churches and others keep a quieter anniversary.

Tradition says that on the eve of All Saints, a friar and teacher named Martin Luther posted a set of theses, points for debate, on the church door in Wittenberg, in Germany, questioning the sale of indulgences, which Catholic teaching describes as release from punishment still due for sins already forgiven.
What followed split Western Christianity. And lately, in some places, Lutherans and Catholics mark it side by side. Today, Reformation Day.

teach.h: THE JUST SHALL LIVE BY FAITH.
teach.b: For Luther, much turned on a verse in Romans, in the King James Bible: "The just shall live by faith." He came to read it as good news: God makes people right as a gift, received by trust, not bought or earned.

Ephesians puts it plainly: "For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God." So when he saw indulgences being sold, he objected. The argument grew far beyond the theses.
The years that followed were bitter, and in places bloody, on more than one side. That history is part of the day, and it's honest to say so.
Then the carry: semper reformanda, a Latin motto later taken up in Reformed churches, often given in full as the church reformed, and always being reformed. Reform isn't a single event in the past.
On this view, a church that thinks it has finished reforming has stopped listening. Paul's line fits: "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." Some readers hear that as ongoing.
Catholics have their own way of saying this: the Second Vatican Council spoke of Christ calling the church to continual reformation, on its pilgrim way.

Lutherans and Catholics have since signed a joint statement on how God makes sinners right, and some now pray together on this day, with thanks for what each has received and sorrow for the wounds of division.
Still different in real ways, on one point they can say the same words: always being reformed.

how: Lutheran and some other Protestant churches keep Reformation Day at the end of October with hymns and readings on grace and faith, and in some places Lutherans and Catholics now hold joint services of prayer.

games.q: you're asked to pray on Reformation Day for a church that needs reform. whose church does the practice point you to?
o: the church as it was long ago.
games.why: your own. semper reformanda turns the question inward: always being reformed, starting at home.

practice: Bring to mind a community you belong to, a church, a family, a team, a workplace, and name one specific thing in it that needs mending: your own, not someone else's. Then name your part in it, however small.
If you pray, ask God to reform your church, beginning with you; if you don't, hold it honestly, without blame.
